transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well... my wife thought I should come in. She thinks I'm making a big deal out of nothing. 

Just... stuff with her work. Late meetings, little changes in her work messages. She says it's just normal office stuff. But... I don't know. For the past year, they've just lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It feels like there's a... a private signal in them. Like it's meant to tell me something she won't just say directly. 

But... yeah. She wanted me to talk to someone, so I'm here.
Besides these suspicions about your wife's messages and meetings, have you ever heard voices, seen things, or sensed a presence that other people couldn't perceive?
No. I don't... hear voices or anything like that. It's just what I said.

When your wife offers an innocent explanation for these messages or meetings, are you able to consider that she might be telling the truth, or do you remain completely certain that something is being hidden from you no matter what she says?

I... I try to listen to her. I know she says it's just normal office stuff. 

But... like I was saying, it’s been a whole year of this. The way these things line up... it's just too precise. I can't just ignore it. I... I really don't think it's an accident. 

So, no, I guess... I can't just accept her explanation. It feels like a signal, no matter what she tells me.
Aside from your wife, have you noticed similar patterns or hidden messages involving other people in your life—like coworkers, friends, or strangers—or does this feeling stay focused only on her?
Um... no. It's... it's just her. I haven't noticed anything like that with anyone else. Just... what I already told you about.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre delusional belief that his wife is sending him hidden signals of infidelity through her work schedule and messages, persisting for about one year. The delusion is encapsulated—confined solely to his wife and not generalized to other relationships. He denies any hallucinations (auditory, visual, or other perceptual disturbances), and there is no evidence of disorganized speech, negative symptoms, or broader psychotic disorganization. The delusion is resistant to counter-evidence (he cannot accept his wife's benign explanations despite trying to listen), consistent with true delusional conviction rather than overvalued idea. This clinical picture—an isolated, systematized delusion of jealousy/infidelity without other psychotic features—is classic for Delusional Disorder (F22), jealous subtype, rather than Schizophrenia (which requires hallucinations, disorganization, or negative symptoms) or unspecified psychosis.
